name: AI/Engagement 4 Internal REVIEWED
content:
# Workshop 4
 
 # Defining Problems with the Public
 
 **Speaker:** [Claudius Lieven](https:/www.hamburg.de/politik-und-verwaltung/behoerden/behoerde-fuer-stadtentwicklung-und-wohnen/themen/stadtentwicklung/stadtwerkstatt/aufgaben-und-ziele/claudius-lieven-187068) (Head of Staff-Unit for Citizen Participation, Ministry of Urban Development and Housing, Hamburg)
 
 Claudius Lieven’s unit sits in the Ministry of Urban Development and Housing. Their motto is “auf Dialogue bauen” — building on dialogues. They advise districts, public companies, and authorities on participation, run city-wide participatory processes directly, and develop new methods and tools for citizen engagement. DIPAS is their primary platform.
 
 Lieven presented Hamburg’s [open-source](https:/www.dipas.org/en/about) digital participation system ( [DIPAS](https:/www.dipas.org/en) ) and demonstrated how the city is using AI to analyze citizen contributions at scale. This is part of what Lieven calls the “deliberative mode” of public engagement, which involves collecting opinions and other information from residents to inform planning decisions.
 
 ## The DIPAS system
 
 DIPAS combines an online engagement platform with in-person digital tools, all feeding into a single shared dataset. The system is built on Drupal and uses a template-based approach in which municipalities create reusable procedure templates with default settings, then customize them for individual projects. This allows a small team to support many concurrent processes.
 
 The online participation tool is a map-based interface where citizens place geo-referenced comments. Contributions respond to open questions and specific plans and are attached to predefined categories configured by administrators. Participation is anonymous with no account creation required, and contributions can be filtered by category, date, or other parameters. Users can comment on others’ contributions and express agreement or disagreement with thumbs up/down.
 
 The Touchtable is a mobile interactive table used at in-person events. It displays the same map and contribution data as the online platform. Participants can explore 2D maps and 3D city models, view each other’s contributions, and draw directly on the map to sketch spatial suggestions. Facilitators can export these drawings as GeoJSON or KML files. Contributions made at in-person events feed into the same shared dataset as online contributions.
 
 Evaluation tools include AI-powered analysis (see below).
 
 [The Navigator](https:/beteiligung.hamburg/navigator/#) aggregates all DIPAS processes citywide into a single public-facing interface. It shows ongoing, completed, and upcoming participation processes on an interactive map alongside KPIs like contribution counts and participation intensity by topic or location.
 
 The system is open source and [has been adopted by nine German cities](https:/hamburg-business.com/en/news/hamburg-makes-dipas-open-source-application-available-nationwide) , including Munich.
 
 ## The AI pipeline
 
 The city developed an open-source AI toolbox, DIPAS Analytics, to analyze textual contributions. Lieven noted that statistical analysis (visualizing where comments come from, which get the most votes) covers maybe 20% of the work. The other 80% is working through text itself, and with 11,000+ contributions every year, manual reading doesn’t scale.
 
 [The pipeline uses:](https:/rebootdemocracy.ai/blog/how-hamburg-is-turning-resident-comments-into-actionable-insight)
 
 (1) Flair for Named Entity Recognition (removing personal data like names and phone numbers)
 
 (2) Llama 3.1 for key message extraction, category assignment, etc.
 
 (3) RoBERTa (German-language BERT variant) for statement labeling
 
 (4) K-means clustering with silhouette scoring for grouping messages
 
 So the pipeline involves: identifying key messages within posts, assigning to predefined categories, aggregating into “aspects” (sub-clusters), then aggregating aspects into clusters. All of this can be represented spatially on the map.
 
 ## 
 
 ## Altona example
 
 Altona’s train station has a contested history. A grand 1898 neo-Romanesque building, somewhat of a local landmark, was demolished in the late 1970s to make way for S-Bahn construction. What replaced it is a brutalist concrete block, widely disliked.
 
 Now, long-distance trains are relocating to a new station at Diebsteich in 2027, and the question is what will happen to the current site.
 
 [Hamburg ran a multi-format participation process](https:/bahnhof-altona.beteiligung.hamburg/#/custompage) to answer that question: online contributions through DIPAS (about 400 submissions, 3,500 ratings), a physical "participatory shop" in the station where around 1,000 people dropped in over three weeks, youth workshops with students from nearby schools, co-creative design sessions, and a public "glass workshop" in November where 350 people engaged directly with five planning teams.
 
 The AI analysis came in on the online component. When they ran the contributions through the pipeline, "urban design" emerged as the dominant topic. But people weren't really answering the question Hamburg had asked about public spaces around the station. They kept circling back to the building itself: identity, historical character, what the station means to the district. The 1970s demolition is still an unresolved loss.
 
 Because the analysis was fast, planners could incorporate this feedback before the subsequent urban design competition brief was finalized. The design teams are now explicitly addressing identity and historic connection, something that might have been missed if staff had to read every contribution manually.
 
 ## Keys to participation in Hamburg
 
 Lieven lists multiple reasons for the success of participation with DIPAS in Hamburg.
 
 One key to unlocking participation is low barriers. The platform requires no registration. IP addresses are not stored on the server, and the AI pipeline includes automated processes to strip personal data from contributions before analysis. The system is digitally barrier-free and screen reader compatible. Notably, this has not resulted in hate speech or trolling despite anonymous participation.
 
 Another key to success is the platform’s transparency. It uses [open-source code](https:/www.dipas.org/en/about) , open data, and published methods, and the processes are kept up-to-date.
 
 The project has also been continuous. It has operated for ten years and supported 133 processes. DIPAS is now familiar to both administrators and citizens.
 
 The platform also has a small internal support team of 2-3 people that provides “attentive service” to districts and agencies using the system.
 
 ## Civil society adoption
 
 [A citizen’s initiative called Lokalkraft](https:/abpflastern.beteilige.me/#) deployed DIPAS independently for “Abpflastern” (unsealing), a project asking residents to identify paved areas that should be converted to permeable surfaces for rainwater absorption (the “sponge city” concept, originating in the Netherlands). The project collected about 2,000 suggestions. The Ministry of Environment has now partnered with them. Lieven presented this as the first instance of bottom-up, private-public co-creation using their tools.
 
 ### 
 
 ## Project metrics
 
 | Total contributions since 2016 | 80,000+ |
 |-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
 | Processes run | 133/10yrs |
 | 2024 contributions (geo-referenced submissions like ideas, comments, or suggestions, but not ratings) | 11,735 |
 | Growth trend | 5,557 (2022) → 11,111 (2023) → 11,735 (2024) |
 | Processes per year | ~16 |
 | Central team | 3 people (Lieven + 2 for attentive service) |
 | Typical engagement window | ~4 weeks online, within a 6-month to 1-year planning cycle |
 | Altona case stats | 402 contributions, 3,533 ratings, 538 aspects, 57 clusters in the urban design category |
 
 ## Takeaways for learners
 
 DIPAS is somewhat rare in that it is an AI-assisted engagement system with a long public track record. Ten years, used in multiple cities, open-source, with public methodology.
 
 Altona is an interesting case. City asked about public space; citizens responded with ideas on the building’s identity and design instead. AI surfaced patterns across 400 comments. Planners reframed the design competition in response. Good example of synthesis at scale.
 
 Operational efficiency. Three people, ~16 processes a year, 11,000+ contributions. Reusable template architecture and shared online/in-person dataset make that possible.
 
 Transparency (open data, open source, transparent processes and updated engagements) and low barriers (digitally barrier-free and anonymous) help engagement and encourage uptake by other cities.
 
 Civil society adoption. Lokalkraft ran their own campaign using DIPAS independently. Rare outcome of genuine openness.
 
 Gap to note: Not clear how planners prioritize feedback or track impact.
 
 ## Audience notes
 
 ### Questions
 
 “How do you communicate the addition of a new project?”
 
 “Do you track impact/how projects changed through participation?”
 
 “How do you prioritize which project feedback to act on?”
 
 “Is there a way to visualize who is most impacted by changes?”
 
 “Do other Hamburg participation processes (outside urban development) use the same AI?”
 
 ## Quotes
 
 ### Claudius Lieven (Hamburg)
 
 "It's just so, 20% of the task solved by doing a statistical analysis, 80% is here in the textual data."
 
 "This was for us a moment of aha, because we explicitly asked another question. We asked, give us feedback to the public spaces around the building, but the citizens said, no, we don't want to talk about the building."
 
 "The citizens really use it in a very deliberate way, and provide information."
 
 "We cannot directly say, okay, we reduced the staff broadly, but we can say, and we can see, we increased the activity broadly. So with the same personnel, we see there can a lot more be done than before."
 
 "The use of AI in evaluating citizen contributions requires sensitive communication."
 
 "We hope this leads us to the possibility of becoming more or less a learning city, to have a better feedback loop from what the citizens think and perceive."
